posts.note: Part 1 of a series on the Clancy mistrial (Sept 4, 2026). Legal-process calls (status hearing, retrial likely, NCR means confinement) plus several own-newsletter series promises (four articles, Part 2 next week, what each expert will say). Interviewee statements not adopted by the author were not logged.

Part 2. Mostly clinical description and interview dialogue; forward-looking items are an implicit DSM-6 presupposition, a 'second jury would be asked' conditional, a present-tense 'will kill' epidemiology claim (flagged not forward-looking), and Part 3 series promises. Normative 'legal standards need to evolve' not logged.

9/11 anniversary essay on repeated blast exposure in special operations forces. Nearly all descriptive or normative; two borderline items logged (collective-memory 'will remember' claim, own content promise). No regulatory, trial, company or payer calls.

statements.quote: On September 29, a status hearing on the case will be heard by the judge, and the district attorney, Timothy Cruz, will decide whether they are going to move ahead with a second trial addressing the same facts with different jurors.
statements.context: After the September 4, 2026 mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy case (Plymouth Superior Court, Massachusetts; jury split 11-1 per the defense), the author states a status hearing is set for September 29 and that district attorney Timothy Cruz will decide then whether to retry the case with a new jury.
statements.note: Reports a scheduled court date; the forecastable part is that the DA decides on a second trial at or around that hearing.

statements.quote: Over the course of four subsequent articles, I will lay out what I learned, weaving together the interviews that I did.
statements.context: 'My Editorial Process' section. The author plans a four-part follow-up series in The Frontier Psychiatrists built from his interviews with Chris Aiken, Will Sauve, David Carreon, Carlene MacMillan and Catherine Birndorf about the Clancy case.
statements.horizon_text: Over the course of four subsequent articles
statements.note: Own-newsletter plan (series length: four more articles). Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: I have deliberately removed any opinions of my interviewees on what the verdict should be, because a re-trial is likely, or at least plausible.
statements.context: Same 'My Editorial Process' section. The author's stated reason for cutting his guests' opinions on the verdict: he expects a second Clancy trial, which he rates 'likely, or at least plausible'.
statements.note: Hedged call on a retrial; the DA's decision is described elsewhere in the post as pending at the September 29 status hearing.

statements.quote: When unanimity is the only acceptable answer, that means we’re not done yet as a society, and Lindsay Clancy is not done yet with this legal matter.
statements.context: After describing the four-option verdict menu and the reported 11-1 split for not criminally responsible, the author asserts that the Clancy legal proceedings will continue.
statements.note: Implicit forecast that proceedings continue; restates the retrial expectation from the editorial-process section.

statements.quote: And if she’s found not guilty by reason of insanity — she’s going to a state psychiatric hospital for God knows how long.
statements.context: The author's own line (labeled 'Owen') in dialogue with Will Sauve. Conditional: if Clancy receives an insanity / not criminally responsible verdict, she will be committed to a state psychiatric hospital for an indefinite period.
statements.note: Conditional on a future verdict; author's own words in interview dialogue.

statements.quote: Even being found not criminally responsible in this matter does not mean freedom for Lindsay Clancy. It means spending as many years as the doctors and judges subsequently deem wise. There is no verdict that means that Lindsay Clancy gets away with anything
statements.context: Follows the author's description of civil commitment after a not-criminally-responsible verdict (at least six months, annual renewals, no maximum while illness and dangerousness persist) and the Hinckley precedent (34 years at St. Elizabeths). The author asserts that any verdict in Clancy's case, including NCR, results in years of confinement.
statements.horizon_text: as many years as the doctors and judges subsequently deem wise
statements.note: Compound: NCR verdict implies long hospitalization; no possible verdict yields freedom. Conditional on a future verdict in a retrial.

statements.quote: Some of those experts, and their frank thoughts, follow over the next four articles.
statements.context: Close of 'The Goldwater Rule' section. The author again says the interviewed experts' views will appear over the next four articles of the series.
statements.note: Restatement of the four-article series plan. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Next week, in Part 2, I ask the question the jury couldn’t answer: was Lindsay Clancy psychotic?
statements.context: Closing section of Part 1. Part 2 of the series is promised for the following week and is to address whether Clancy was psychotic.
statements.note: Own-newsletter schedule and content promise. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Catherine Birndorf will explain why this illness almost never looks the way jurors expect.
statements.context: Preview of Part 2 (promised for 'next week'): Catherine Birndorf of The Motherhood Center is to explain that postpartum psychosis rarely presents the way jurors expect.
statements.note: Content promise for Part 2 of the author's own series. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: David Carreon will explain why a voice that arrives only once, for 45 minutes, and never returns is, his words, “unheard of.”
statements.context: Preview of Part 2: David Carreon (Acacia Clinics) is to argue that a single 45-minute command hallucination that never recurs is unheard of.
statements.note: Content promise for Part 2 of the author's own series. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Chris Aiken will point to the diagnostic clue that was sitting in the chart the whole time: three days without sleep, on sertraline.
statements.context: Preview of Part 2: Chris Aiken (Carlat Psychiatry Report) is to flag three days of insomnia on sertraline as a missed diagnostic clue in the Clancy record.
statements.note: Content promise for Part 2 of the author's own series. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Of note, our guest Dr. Birndorf is on the task force advocating for its reinstatement when DSM-6 comes to pass.
statements.context: Epidemiology paragraph: postpartum psychosis was removed from the DSM in 1980 and is absent from DSM-5-TR. The author notes Catherine Birndorf sits on a task force seeking its reinstatement in a future DSM-6.
statements.note: Borderline: presupposes a DSM-6 will be published; reinstatement itself is third-party advocacy, not an author prediction.

statements.quote: So, while rare, these brain disorders are also the most common thing that will kill a new mother.
statements.context: The author's own paragraph on the word 'rare': citing CDC data that mental health conditions account for 23% of pregnancy-related deaths, he states they are the most common thing that will kill a new mother, ahead of hemorrhage and cardiomyopathy.
statements.note: Present-tense epidemiological claim phrased with 'will'; describes the current leading cause, not a forecast of change. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: The category is worth understanding on its own terms: whether hearing a command compels obeying it is precisely the question a second jury would be asked to weigh.
statements.context: Author's bridging paragraph before David Carreon's comments on command auditory hallucinations. It presupposes a second Clancy trial and predicts that its central question will be whether a command hallucination compels obedience.
statements.note: Conditional/implicit: assumes a retrial happens; restates Part 1's 're-trial is likely' expectation.

statements.quote: That is not a courtroom problem. That is a care problem, and it’s where this series goes next.
statements.context: Closing of the analysis section. The author says the next installment of the series will turn from the courtroom to the care system that treated Clancy.
statements.note: Own-newsletter content plan. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Next Week: If This Was Good Care, What Does That Say About Care? Stay tuned for the next part in this ongoing series. Here are some previews from the upcoming Part 3…
statements.context: Part 3 is announced for the following week under the title 'If This Was Good Care, What Does That Say About Care?', with pull-quotes from David Carreon, Chris Aiken and Carlene MacMillan given as previews.
statements.note: Own-newsletter schedule and title promise; heading plus following paragraph joined after whitespace normalization. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Most of us will remember Covid-19 as something that changed the world. For the military, it was September 11.
statements.context: Opening reflection on the 25th anniversary of September 11, 2001. The author contrasts how civilians will remember Covid-19 as the world-changing event while for service members it was 9/11.
statements.note: Borderline, truism-like claim about collective memory; logged for recall.

statements.quote: I’m going to write about one of those hidden wounds. This will not be about Post-traumatic stress disorder.
statements.context: After describing Homebase (a Massachusetts General Hospital and Boston Red Sox Foundation program for special operations forces), the author announces his topic: a hidden wound of warriors other than PTSD, which the rest of the post identifies as repeated blast exposure.
statements.note: Own-newsletter content promise, largely fulfilled within the same post (repeated blast exposure). Coder may mark CONTROL.
